DERMATOLOGY__Skin Cancer & Pre-malignant:
Overview — skin cancer & pre-malignant lesions
The common skin malignancies — BCC, SCC and melanoma — together with pre-malignant lesions (actinic keratosis, Bowen's disease) and melanoma in situ (lentigo maligna). Most are UV-driven.
The organising principle: split into non-melanoma (BCC, SCC) vs melanoma. BCC = commonest, locally invasive, rarely metastasises; SCC = can metastasise, arises in sun-damaged skin / AK / Bowen's; melanoma = most dangerous — assess with ABCDE, and Breslow thickness is the key prognostic factor.

What & Why

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC, “rodent ulcer”) = the COMMONEST skin cancer — a locally invasive, SLOW-growing malignancy of the basal keratinocytes, driven by cumulative UV. Classic lesion: a ROLLED (pearly) edge, central ULCER, and TELANGIECTASIA.

The core concept — locally invasive but almost NEVER metastasises: dangerous through local destruction (erodes tissue — hence “rodent ulcer”), not distant spread → low-mortality but high-morbidity. Neglected facial BCC invades cartilage/bone/eye/nose. Tasks: recognise (pearly rolled edge + telangiectasia), identify subtype, refer, excise.
Very common; increases with age + cumulative sun; face is the classic site. Reflex: a slow-growing, pearly, rolled-edged nodule with telangiectasia (± central ulcer) on sun-exposed skin of an older adult = BCC → refer for excision.

Risk Factors
☀️ Main driver
  • Cumulative UV, sunburn, sunbeds; fair skin (Fitzpatrick 1–2), older age, outdoor occupation
🧬 Other
  • Immunosuppression (transplant), radiotherapy, arsenic
  • Genetic: Gorlin (basal cell naevus) syndrome (multiple/young BCCs), xeroderma pigmentosum
The rule: BCC risk = cumulative UV / fair skin / age + immunosuppression; multiple/young BCCs → think Gorlin syndrome.
Investigations & Referral
A CLINICAL (± dermoscopic) diagnosis, confirmed HISTOLOGICALLY. A diagnostic incisional/punch biopsy may be taken first to determine the growth pattern (subtype) before definitive excision, esp. for larger/high-risk lesions. CT/MRI only for suspected deep invasion (bone/nerve/orbit).
Referral (NICE): suspected BCC → usually a ROUTINE referral (slow-growing, rarely metastasises — NOT routinely 2-week-wait). Consider a 2-week-wait ONLY if delay would have significant impact (critical site — near eye/nose — or large size). SCC or melanoma → 2-week-wait (BCC is the exception).
Management
The principle: surgical EXCISION is the treatment of choice; Mohs for high-risk/facial/recurrent; non-surgical if surgery unsuitable; topical/PDT for the superficial subtype.
🔪 Surgery
  • Standard excision = treatment of choice — ~4mm margin (low-risk), ≥5mm (high-risk)
  • MOHS micrographic surgery (staged, real-time margins) for HIGH-RISK: facial/cosmetic sites, recurrent, morphoeic/infiltrative, ill-defined margins
🧴 Non-surgical
  • Curettage + cautery; radiotherapy — if surgery unsuitable/declined
  • Superficial subtype: photodynamic therapy, imiquimod, topical 5-fluorouracil, cryotherapy
Follow-up: do NOT routinely follow up an adequately-excised isolated BCC (advise sun protection + self-monitoring); follow up high-risk/multiple/incompletely-excised.

What it is
BCC (“rodent ulcer”) = COMMONEST skin cancer; locally invasive but RARELY metastasises (danger = local destruction); UV-driven, sun-exposed sites, older/fair.
Features
PEARLY, ROLLED edge + TELANGIECTASIA ± central ULCER; slow-growing; can be pigmented.
Subtypes
Nodular (classic) · superficial (topical-amenable) · MORPHOEIC (scar-like, high-risk) · pigmented (melanoma mimic).
Referral
ROUTINE (NOT 2WW) — 2WW only if site/size means delay matters; multiple/young → GORLIN.
Management
Surgical EXCISION (4mm low / ≥5mm high) = 1st-line; MOHS (high-risk/facial/recurrent/morphoeic); curettage-cautery/radiotherapy if unsuitable; superficial → PDT/imiquimod/5-FU/cryo; don't routinely follow up isolated excised BCC.
What & Why

Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) = the second commonest skin cancer — a malignancy of the epidermal KERATINOCYTES, UV-driven, presenting as an exophytic, RAPIDLY-growing, KERATOTIC nodule on sun-exposed skin, often arising in a pre-existing actinic keratosis or Bowen's disease.

The core concept — SCC CAN METASTASISE (BCC essentially doesn't) → the more dangerous keratinocyte cancer, needing more urgent handling (2-week-wait). It grows rapidly over weeks, is keratotic/scaly/crusted, ulcerates, and is often tender/bleeds. Three threads: (1) a UV-damage SPECTRUM (actinic keratosis → Bowen's → invasive SCC); (2) recognise HIGH-RISK features; (3) 2-week-wait + excision.
Sites: face, lips, ears, hands, limbs; older, fair-skinned, sun-damaged. Reflex: a rapidly-growing, keratotic, tender/bleeding nodule on sun-exposed skin (esp. in actinic damage) = SCC → 2-week-wait → excision.

Clinical Features & Variants
🔎 The lesion
  • Enlarging scaly/crusted lumps, growing RAPIDLY over weeks; may ulcerate; often tender/painful/bleed
  • Arise in pre-existing actinic keratosis / Bowen's; sites — face, lips, ears, hands, limbs
🔀 Variants
  • Keratoacanthoma — rapidly-growing crateriform nodule with a central keratin plug (well-differentiated SCC variant; treat as SCC)
  • Marjolin's ulcer — SCC arising in a chronic wound/scar/ulcer/burn
The rule: a rapidly-enlarging, keratotic/crusted, tender/bleeding nodule (± ulceration) on sun-exposed skin, often in actinic damage = SCC.
Risk Factors & High-Risk Features
Risk factors
  • Cumulative UV + fair skin + age (main); IMMUNOSUPPRESSION (transplant — markedly ↑ + more aggressive)
  • Chronic wounds/scars (Marjolin's), HPV, radiation, arsenic; xeroderma pigmentosum
🚩 High-risk features
  • Site: LIP, EAR, temple; size >2 cm; thickness >4–6 mm
  • Poorly differentiated; perineural invasion; immunosuppression; recurrent; in a scar
The rule: high-risk SCC (lip/ear, large/thick, poorly differentiated, perineural, immunosuppressed, recurrent) → higher metastatic risk → wider margins + MDT. Transplant patients get more frequent + aggressive SCCs.
Investigations, Referral & Management
Investigations: clinical diagnosis, confirmed HISTOLOGICALLY; assess regional LYMPH NODES (can metastasise) — imaging (US/CT ± FNA) if nodal/deep spread suspected. Referral: suspected SCC → 2-WEEK-WAIT (contrast BCC = routine).
🔪 Treatment
  • Surgical EXCISION = gold standard — ~4mm (low-risk), ≥6mm (high-risk); involved/close margins → MDT ± re-excision
  • MOHS for high-risk sites (face/lip/ear), ill-defined, recurrent; radiotherapy if non-surgical/adjuvant
🚑 High-risk / advanced
  • Skin cancer MDT; nodal disease → lymph node dissection ± radiotherapy
  • Advanced/metastatic → immunotherapy (cemiplimab, anti-PD-1 — NICE-approved)
  • Treat precursors (actinic keratosis/Bowen's); sun protection + surveillance (esp. immunosuppressed)
Follow-up: high-risk SCC → follow-up (recurrence/nodal surveillance); low-risk completely-excised → minimal.

2nd commonest skin cancer (keratinocyte); UV-driven; exophytic, RAPIDLY-growing, KERATOTIC/crusted nodule that ulcerates + is tender/bleeds; face/lips/ears/hands.
KEY vs BCC
SCC = rapid, keratotic, tender, CAN METASTASISE → 2-WEEK-WAIT; BCC = slow, pearly, rarely metastasises → routine.
Spectrum

Variants

Management
2WW → surgical EXCISION (4mm low / ≥6mm high); MOHS (high-risk/facial); radiotherapy; MDT + node dissection + cemiplimab (advanced); assess LYMPH NODES.
What & Why

Malignant melanoma = a malignant tumour of MELANOCYTES — the most dangerous skin cancer because it METASTASISES readily. Less common than BCC/SCC but causes the majority of skin-cancer DEATHS; incidence rising; the commonest cancer in the 15–34 age range.

The core concept — metastatic potential: melanoma spreads early + widely (lymph nodes → lung/liver/brain/bone), so EARLY detection is everything and prognosis depends overwhelmingly on how DEEP it is (BRESLOW THICKNESS) at excision. Approach: (1) RECOGNISE early (ABCDE + 7-point checklist + “ugly duckling”); (2) refer URGENTLY (2-week-wait) + excision biopsy; (3) STAGE by BRESLOW; (4) modern immunotherapy/targeted therapy for advanced disease.
Risk: UV (esp. intermittent intense sun/sunburn, sunbeds), fair skin, many/atypical moles, family history, immunosuppression.

What & Why

Actinic keratosis (solar keratosis) = a PRE-cancerous epidermal lesion — scaly, erythematous patches on sun-exposed skin of seniors. Bowen's disease = SCC IN SITU — a chronic, slowly-enlarging red, scaly plaque. Both are steps on the UV-damage → SCC spectrum.

The core concept — a continuum of increasing dysplasia toward invasive SCC, distinguished by DEPTH: actinic keratosis = PARTIAL-thickness epidermal dysplasia (pre-malignant); Bowen's = FULL-thickness (carcinoma in situ) — neither has breached the basement membrane (so neither metastasises). Importance: (1) markers of significant sun damage/field risk; (2) each can PROGRESS to invasive SCC.
Reflex: scaly rough patches = actinic keratosis (pre-cancer); a persistent red scaly plaque = Bowen's (SCC in situ) → treat + watch for a nodule/induration = invasive SCC.

Actinic Keratosis — Features & Management
🔎 Features
  • Rough, scaly, “sandpaper-like” erythematous patches (often better FELT than seen); ± cutaneous horn
  • Sun-exposed sites — face, bald scalp, ears, dorsum of hands, forearms; usually multiple; small SCC risk each
💊 Management
  • Few discrete lesions: cryotherapy, curettage + cautery, excision
  • Multiple / field: topical 5-fluorouracil (Efudix), imiquimod, diclofenac gel, tirbanibulin, or PDT
  • Mild: emollients + sun protection + observation
The rule: few → cryotherapy/curettage; multiple/field → topical 5-FU (Efudix)/imiquimod/diclofenac/PDT; strict sun protection; watch for progression to SCC.
Bowen's Disease — Features & Management
🔎 Features
  • A well-demarcated, red, scaly/crusted PLAQUE — flat, slowly enlarging over months–years
  • Mimics eczema/psoriasis but is PERSISTENT + solitary + doesn't respond to steroids; lower legs (older women), sun-exposed, head/neck; HPV → genital Bowen's
💊 Management
  • BIOPSY confirms + excludes invasion. Options: topical 5-FU/imiquimod, cryotherapy, PDT, curettage, or excision
  • Lower leg heals poorly → PDT/topicals preferred over surgery/cryo; observation reasonable for small/stable in the frail elderly
The rule: a persistent, solitary, red scaly plaque failing to respond to steroids → suspect Bowen's → biopsy; a nodule/induration/ulceration within it → INVASIVE SCC → biopsy + treat as SCC (2WW/excision).
Referral & Exam Pearls
Referral: actinic keratosis + Bowen's = usually primary care / ROUTINE dermatology referral (pre-invasive — NOT 2-week-wait). BUT if invasive SCC is suspected (nodule/induration/ulceration/rapid change within them) → 2-WEEK-WAIT.
Spectrum
Actinic keratosis (PARTIAL-thickness, PRE-malignant, scaly patch) → Bowen's (FULL-thickness, SCC IN SITU, red scaly plaque) → invasive SCC (nodule, can metastasise).
Actinic keratosis
Rough “sandpaper” patches on sun-exposed skin, older/fair; few = cryotherapy/curettage; multiple/field = 5-FU (Efudix)/imiquimod/diclofenac/PDT; sun protection.
Bowen's = SCC in situ
Persistent red scaly PLAQUE (mimics eczema/psoriasis, no steroid response); lower legs; HPV → genital → biopsy; 5-FU/imiquimod, cryo, PDT (preferred on legs), excision.
Watch + refer
A NODULE/INDURATION/ULCERATION within them → INVASIVE SCC → biopsy + 2WW; otherwise routine referral.
What & Why

Lentigo maligna = melanoma IN SITU on chronically sun-damaged skin — malignant melanocytes confined to the epidermis — a long-standing, VERY slowly-growing pigmented patch, classically on the face of the elderly. Invasive form (into the dermis) = lentigo maligna MELANOMA.

The core concept — the “in situ” stage of one melanoma subtype (the melanocytic parallel to Bowen's). An indolent, radial in-situ proliferation of atypical melanocytes confined to the epidermis → grows VERY slowly over years, without metastatic potential while in situ. Importance: (1) can PROGRESS to invasive lentigo maligna melanoma (which metastasises); (2) often large + ill-defined on the FACE → management balances cure vs cosmesis.
Reflex: a slowly-enlarging, irregular, variably-pigmented flat patch on the sun-damaged face of an elderly person = lentigo maligna → biopsy → excise/treat + watch for a nodule signalling invasion.

Clinical Features & Investigations
🔎 Features
  • A flat, irregular, variably-pigmented (tan/brown/black) MACULE/patch, enlarging slowly over YEARS; ill-defined, asymmetric borders
  • Chronically sun-damaged face (cheek, temple, nose) of the ELDERLY; often large by presentation
🔬 Investigations
  • Dermoscopy (distinguishes from benign lentigo/seborrhoeic keratosis)
  • Biopsy — of the most atypical/thickest area (detect any invasion); distinguish from solar lentigo, seborrhoeic keratosis, pigmented actinic keratosis
The rule: shows ABCDE features but evolves very slowly; dermoscopy + biopsy (assess the thickest/most atypical area for invasion).
Management & Referral
The principle: surgical EXCISION is the treatment of choice (in situ margin ≥0.5cm); non-surgical (radiotherapy/imiquimod) for large/facial/unsuitable; if invasive → treat as melanoma by Breslow.
🔪 Surgery — first-line
  • Complete excision with a clinical margin of ≥0.5 cm (as for melanoma in situ / stage 0)
  • Often large + ill-defined on the face → Mohs / staged (“slow Mohs”) excision for facial/cosmetic sites
🧴 Non-surgical / invasive
  • If surgery unsuitable: radiotherapy, or off-label topical imiquimod; observation in the very frail
  • If invasive (lentigo maligna melanoma): wide local excision by BRESLOW (in situ ≥0.5cm / stage I ≥1cm / stage II 2cm) ± SLNB if Breslow >1mm
Referral: suspected lentigo maligna / lentigo maligna melanoma → 2-WEEK-WAIT (it's a melanoma — even in situ, refer urgently). Sun protection + surveillance.
Exam Pearls
What it is
Melanoma IN SITU on sun-damaged skin (melanocytes confined to the epidermis); long-standing, VERY slow pigmented patch on the FACE of the ELDERLY.
vs Lentigo maligna melanoma
LMM = invaded the dermis → metastasises (Breslow applies); a NODULE/thickening within the flat patch = invasion.
Features
Flat, irregular, variably-pigmented macule enlarging over YEARS; ABCDE but very slow; often large; distinguish from solar lentigo / seborrhoeic keratosis / pigmented actinic keratosis.
Investigations
Dermoscopy + biopsy (assess thickest/most atypical area for invasion).
Management
EXCISION (≥0.5cm; Mohs/staged for face); radiotherapy or topical imiquimod if unsuitable; if invasive → wide local excision by BRESLOW ± SLNB. Referral = 2-week-wait (it's a melanoma).
DERMATOLOGY__Immunobullous Disorders:
Overview — immunobullous disorders
Autoimmune blistering diseases in which autoantibodies target skin adhesion proteins. The level of the split determines the blister type and fragility.
The organising principle: where the antibody attacks. Pemphigus = intra-epidermal (desmoglein) → flaccid, fragile blisters, positive Nikolsky, mucosa involved; bullous pemphigoid = sub-epidermal (hemidesmosome/BP180) → tense, robust blisters, elderly; dermatitis herpetiformis = sub-epidermal IgA, itchy grouped vesicles, coeliac-associated.
DiseaseLevel / antibodyClinical & association
Pemphigus vulgarisintra-epidermal, anti-desmoglein 3flaccid blisters, +Nikolsky, painful mucosal erosions; middle-aged
Bullous pemphigoidsub-epidermal, anti-BP180/230tense itchy blisters, elderly; mucosa usually spared
Dermatitis herpetiformissub-epidermal, IgAintensely itchy grouped vesicles (extensors); coeliac → gluten-free diet + dapsone
Pemphigus vulgaris can be life-threatening (fluid loss/infection, like a burn). Confirm with skin biopsy + direct immunofluorescence. In dermatitis herpetiformis, screen for coeliac disease.
What & Why

Bullous pemphigoid = an autoimmune blistering condition — the commonest autoimmune bullous disease — in which antibodies attack the DEEP anchoring proteins of the basement membrane → producing TENSE, sub-epidermal blisters in the elderly.

The core concept — WHERE the split is: autoantibodies target the hemidesmosome proteins BP180 + BP230 that anchor the epidermis to the dermis at the basement membrane → the split is DEEP (sub-epidermal) → the full-thickness epidermis lifts off as an intact ROOF → TENSE, robust blisters. This deep, roof-intact split explains everything: tense (not fragile) blisters, Nikolsky NEGATIVE, and mucosa usually spared.
Contrast pemphigus (anti-desmoglein → superficial split → flaccid blisters, Nikolsky positive, mucosal erosions). A disease of the elderly (>60), with notable neurological + drug associations. Reflex: tense, itchy blisters on an elderly patient (± preceding urticated/eczematous plaques) = bullous pemphigoid.

Memory hook: “pemphi-GOID = GOOD/tense (deep, roof intact); pemphi-GUS = GRoss/flaccid + mucosa (superficial)” — or “the deeper the antibody, the tenser the blister”.
Pathophysiology & Associations
Mechanism: anti-BP180/BP230 antibodies bind hemidesmosomes → complement + inflammation → sub-epidermal split → tense blister.
🧠 Associations
  • Age >60
  • Neurological disease — stroke, dementia, Parkinson's disease
  • Uncommonly, underlying malignancy
💊 Drug triggers

  • PD-1 inhibitors (immunotherapy for metastatic melanoma)

What & Why

SJS / TEN = a severe, life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction — a spectrum of epidermal necrosis + detachment with mucosal involvement, most often a DRUG reaction: dusky erythema → full-thickness necrosis + desquamation, with extensive ocular + oral involvement.

The core concept: SJS and TEN are the SAME disease at different severities — a type IV hypersensitivity reaction (cytotoxic T-cell/keratinocyte apoptosis) in which the epidermis dies + sheds off the dermis in sheets, like a superficial burn. Two things make it an emergency: (1) the SKIN FAILS as an organ → massive fluid/electrolyte loss, thermoregulatory failure + a huge portal for infection/sepsis (the leading cause of death); and (2) MUCOSAL involvement (eyes, mouth, GU, airway) → blindness, strictures, airway compromise.
The single most important action is STOP THE CULPRIT DRUG, then supportive care in an HDU/burns unit. The reflex: a drug + a spreading painful rash with blistering/skin peeling + mucosal ulceration + Nikolsky's sign = SJS/TEN → stop the drug + burns-unit care.

Necrotising fasciitis = a rapidly progressive, life-threatening bacterial infection of the DEEP soft tissues — spreading along the fascial planes with necrosis of fascia + subcutaneous fat — a surgical EMERGENCY.

The core concept — a lethal mismatch: the surface looks far better than the disaster underneath. The infection tracks rapidly along the deep (avascular) fascia, thrombosing the vessels to the overlying skin → so early on the skin can look deceptively normal/mildly cellulitic while beneath it the tissue is dying + the patient is becoming septic. Two hallmarks: (1) PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION (the earliest, most important clue) and (2) rapid systemic toxicity/sepsis.
It advances by the hour + kills → recognise early → resuscitate → BROAD-SPECTRUM ANTIBIOTICS → URGENT SURGICAL DEBRIDEMENT (antibiotics alone don't work — the dead, avascular tissue must be cut out). DELAY = DEATH. The diagnosis is clinical/surgical — do NOT wait for imaging.

The malignancy point: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides / Sézary syndrome) is the important malignant cause → in an older patient with erythroderma + lymphadenopathy, look for Sézary cells on blood film.
Clinical Features
🔴 Skin
  • >90% BSA widespread bright red, warm skin with scaling/exfoliation; intense itch; skin feels tight; later thickening/lichenification
  • Clues to cause: nail/scalp changes (psoriasis), flexural (eczema), islands of sparing (pityriasis rubra pilaris), lymphadenopathy (lymphoma)
💔 Systemic (skin failure)
  • Hypothermia (lost thermoregulation)
  • Fluid/electrolyte loss, dehydration; hypoalbuminaemia + oedema
  • High-output cardiac failure (cutaneous vasodilation)
  • Infection/SEPSIS — the leading cause of death
The rule: erythroderma = red/scaly >90% BSA + systemic effects of SKIN FAILURE (hypothermia, dehydration, hypoalbuminaemia, high-output heart failure, sepsis) — treat like a burn.
Investigations
Assess the systemic effects: temperature, fluid balance, U&E, albumin, FBC, CRP, cultures (sepsis screen).
Find the cause: skin biopsy (may show psoriasis/eczema/lymphoma/pityriasis rubra pilaris); blood film (Sézary cells → cutaneous T-cell lymphoma); eosinophilia (drug/DRESS); drug history.
Management
The principle: admit — emergency supportive care (like a burn) + treat the underlying cause + STOP any culprit drug.
🏥 Supportive (emergency)
  • Fluid + electrolyte replacement, warming (correct hypothermia), monitor/support cardiac function, nutrition, treat/prevent infection
  • Skin care: liberal EMOLLIENTS (mainstay), wet wraps, mild topical steroids, non-adherent dressings
🎯 Treat the cause
  • STOP any culprit drug
  • Eczema/psoriasis → treat the flare (for psoriasis, avoid systemic steroids — rebound; use methotrexate/ciclosporin/biologics)
  • Cutaneous lymphoma (Sézary) → oncology/haematology; pityriasis rubra pilaris → retinoids/methotrexate
The rule: admit → burns-type supportive care (fluids, warming, infection control, emollients) → STOP culprit drugs → treat the underlying cause (careful with systemic steroids in psoriasis).

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) = a superficial blistering condition of young children, caused by exfoliative (epidermolytic) TOXINS released by Staphylococcus aureus → erythema + superficial desquamation with a positive Nikolsky's sign, so the skin looks scalded/burned.

The core concept — TOXIN-mediated, not a direct skin infection: a Staph aureus infection (often at a distant, trivial site — nose, throat, umbilicus, conjunctiva) releases exfoliative toxins A + B into the circulation → these cleave desmoglein-1 (holding upper epidermal cells together) → the superficial epidermis splits + peels in sheets, like a scald.
Two facts: (1) the split is SUPERFICIAL → heals without scarring + spares the mucous membranes (mucosa lacks desmoglein-1); (2) it affects YOUNG CHILDREN/neonates (immature renal toxin clearance + no protective antibodies). Priorities: recognise it, distinguish from TEN, treat with anti-staphylococcal ANTIBIOTICS (good prognosis).

🦠 The toxin mechanism

  • Toxins are proteases that cleave DESMOGLEIN-1 (superficial granular-layer epidermis) → loss of adhesion → superficial split → peeling
👶 Why young children
  • Immature renal clearance of the toxin + lack of protective anti-toxin antibodies
  • So it's a disease of neonates/young children (rarely adults with renal failure/immunocompromise)
The rule: Staph exfoliative toxin → cleaves desmoglein-1 → superficial epidermal split; affects children (poor toxin clearance + no antibodies); mucosa spared (no desmoglein-1).

Skin biopsy (if unclear) shows a SUPERFICIAL (subcorneal/granular-layer) split — vs the full-thickness necrosis of TEN. Bloods: FBC/CRP, hydration/electrolytes.

The principle: anti-staphylococcal ANTIBIOTICS (it responds well) + supportive skin/fluid care; good prognosis.
💊 Antibiotics — definitive
  • IV anti-staph antibiotics (e.g. flucloxacillin) to eradicate the Staph aureus source (± clindamycin to suppress toxin)
  • Responds well (unlike TEN)
🩹 Supportive
  • Fluid + electrolyte management (barrier loss → fluid loss, like a superficial burn), analgesia, temperature control
  • Emollients / non-adherent dressings for denuded skin; avoid steroids
Prognosis: generally GOOD in children — heals WITHOUT scarring (superficial split) within ~1–2 weeks (worse in adults with comorbidity/renal failure).

Eczema herpeticum = a widespread, potentially life-threatening herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection of eczematous (or barrier-damaged) skin — a dermatological EMERGENCY: red, inflamed skin covered with raised scaly patches + small vesicles or pustules.

The core concept: what happens when HSV infects skin whose barrier is already broken by eczema. Normally HSV causes a localised cold sore, but in atopic eczema the impaired barrier + local immune dysfunction let the virus spread widely + rapidly → a disseminated, monomorphic vesicular eruption. Two things make it an emergency: (1) systemic dissemination (viraemia; rarely HSV encephalitis/hepatitis/keratitis) and (2) secondary BACTERIAL superinfection + sepsis.
The single most important action is early recognition → prompt ACICLOVIR (don't wait for confirmation). The reflex: a child (or adult) with eczema that suddenly worsens with clustered/punched-out vesicles + fever + being unwell = eczema herpeticum → aciclovir now.

The “punched-out” point: ruptured vesicles leave numerous small, uniform, round, crusted, “punched-out” erosions — the classic sign. Eczema herpeticum is frequently co-infected with bacteria → often needs BOTH aciclovir AND antibiotics.

  • Active/severe atopic eczema; other barrier-defective skin (Darier's, burns, pemphigus, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma)
  • Young children; immunosuppression

Largely a CLINICAL diagnosis — treat on suspicion, do NOT wait. Start aciclovir empirically while confirming. Confirm: viral swab (from a vesicle) for HSV PCR (± bacterial swab for co-infection).

The principle: prompt ACICLOVIR (± IV if severe/systemic) + treat bacterial co-infection + supportive skin care + ophthalmology if eyes; do NOT delay.

  • Ophthalmology URGENTLY if eyes/periocular involved (HSV keratitis → sight risk)
🩹 Adjuncts
  • Anti-staph/strep antibiotics (flucloxacillin) for bacterial co-infection (common)
  • Analgesia, fluids, continue emollients; be cautious with topical steroids on actively infected skin
  • Admit if systemically unwell, extensive, young/immunocompromised, or eye involvement

Acanthosis nigricans = symmetrical, velvety, hyperpigmented (brown-black) thickening of the skin, classically in the body FOLDS/FLEXURES (axillae, neck, groin) — a cutaneous SIGN of an underlying systemic process, most often INSULIN RESISTANCE.

The core concept: not a disease in itself but a SKIN MARKER. The dominant mechanism is INSULIN RESISTANCE: high circulating insulin cross-activates IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes + fibroblasts → epidermal proliferation → the velvety thickening. So the key response to spotting it: think insulin resistance → screen for type 2 diabetes / obesity / PCOS.
The crucial exception — the malignant form: a rare but dangerous paraneoplastic acanthosis nigricans (usually gastric adenocarcinoma) appears suddenly, extensively + atypically in a non-obese adult → prompting a cancer search. The decisive question: common (benign, insulin-resistance) or rare (malignant, paraneoplastic)?

🔎 The plaques
  • Symmetrical, velvety, hyperpigmented (light brown to black) thickened plaques
  • Flexures: posterior/lateral NECK (commonest), AXILLAE, GROIN, antecubital/popliteal fossae, umbilicus
  • Feel thickened + velvety; don't wash off; usually asymptomatic
🏷️ Company it keeps
  • Often with skin tags (acrochordons) in the same areas — both insulin-resistance signs
The rule: symmetrical velvety brown-black thickening of the neck/axillae/groin (± skin tags) = acanthosis nigricans → look for insulin resistance (and exclude the malignant form).
Investigations
A CLINICAL diagnosis (the characteristic velvety flexural plaques); biopsy rarely needed.
🍬 Insulin resistance / diabetes
  • Fasting glucose, HbA1c, ± fasting insulin/lipids; BMI/weight
  • PCOS work-up if relevant (androgens, LH/FSH, pelvic USS); endocrine screen (Cushing's/acromegaly/TFTs) if suggested
🔎 Malignancy screen
  • If sudden/extensive/atypical/non-obese ± weight loss: examination, endoscopy (gastric), imaging, tumour markers
The rule: check HbA1c/glucose (insulin resistance) in everyone; investigate for malignancy (esp. gastric — endoscopy) if sudden/extensive/atypical.
Management
The principle: treat the UNDERLYING CAUSE — the skin follows; there is no specific “cure” for the plaques themselves.
🎯 Treat the cause
  • Insulin resistance → WEIGHT LOSS + lifestyle + treat diabetes (metformin — improving insulin sensitivity often improves the skin)
  • Stop a causative drug; treat the endocrinopathy / PCOS
  • Malignant form → treat the underlying cancer (may regress with successful treatment)
💅 Skin-directed (cosmetic)
  • Topical retinoids, keratolytics (urea, salicylic acid), topical vitamin D analogues
  • The plaques are otherwise harmless
The rule: treat the cause (weight loss/diabetes control for the common form; treat the cancer for the malignant form) — the skin improves; topical retinoids/keratolytics for cosmesis.

Necrobiosis lipoidica = a chronic granulomatous skin condition producing well-demarcated, shiny, atrophic yellow-brown plaques, classically on the SHINS (pretibial) — strongly associated with DIABETES (historically “necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum”).

The core concept: another cutaneous sign of systemic disease — its importance is the link with diabetes + its tendency to ulcerate. Pathology = degeneration of dermal collagen (“necrobiosis”) + a granulomatous response → an atrophic plaque you can almost see through — waxy, yellow, with visible telangiectasia.
Two threads: (1) it should prompt you to think of / screen for DIABETES (though not all patients are diabetic, and treating diabetes doesn't reliably improve the skin); (2) the plaques are fragile + prone to ULCERATION. Classically on the shins of women; benign but chronic + notoriously hard to treat.

Largely a CLINICAL diagnosis (the characteristic plaque + site). Screen for diabetes: HbA1c / fasting glucose if not already diagnosed.

The principle: benign but chronic + hard to treat — protect the skin + optimise diabetes/risk factors; topical/intralesional steroids first-line; escalate for refractory or ulcerated disease.

  • Potent TOPICAL corticosteroids (to the active border) or intralesional steroids — cautiously on atrophic skin

  • Ulcerated → wound care + protection; treat secondary infection; tissue viability/dermatology

The key lesson: recognise this specific rash → measure GLUCAGON → image the pancreas. Rare, but very high-yield as the pattern-recognition link rash → glucagonoma.

Serum GLUCAGON — markedly RAISED (diagnostic of glucagonoma) — the key test the rash should trigger.

  • Manage the diabetes; VTE prophylaxis (thromboembolism risk); skin/wound care

What & Why

Cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) = the skin manifestations of lupus — a spectrum from skin-limited disease to a cutaneous sign of systemic lupus (SLE). The classic subtypes: acute CLE (the malar rash of SLE), subacute CLE (SCLE), and chronic CLE (discoid lupus, DLE).

The core concept: cutaneous lupus is fundamentally a PHOTOSENSITIVE autoimmune skin disease — the lesions favour sun-exposed areas and are triggered/worsened by UV. Two questions dominate: (1) which SUBTYPE? (morphology, antibodies + scarring risk differ) and (2) is there UNDERLYING SYSTEMIC lupus? — CLE can be skin-only or the visible tip of multisystem disease. Hence the workup always screens ANA + dsDNA.
The scarring + systemic-risk gradient: acute (malar) → strongly SLE-associated, non-scarring; SCLE → anti-Ro, photosensitive, non-scarring; discoid (DLE) → scarring, mostly skin-limited. Management centres on the cornerstone of SUN PROTECTION + hydroxychloroquine.

What & Why

Dermatomyositis = an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy with characteristic SKIN signs — an autoimmune condition causing proximal muscle weakness + a distinctive photosensitive rash. This note focuses on the cutaneous features; the muscle disease is covered in the rheumatology myositis note.

The core concept: dermatomyositis is unique among the inflammatory myopathies in having pathognomonic skin signs — so the rash is often the diagnostic key, and it can precede, accompany, or (in “amyopathic” disease) occur WITHOUT the muscle weakness. The signs are photosensitive (shawl sign, face, hands). Two imperatives: (1) recognise the pathognomonic rash + confirm the myositis, and (2) — critically — SCREEN FOR UNDERLYING MALIGNANCY, because adult dermatomyositis is strongly paraneoplastic.
Bimodal (children + adults); the adult form carries the crucial cancer association. Management = steroids + immunosuppression + sun protection.

What & Why

Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis (CSVV) = inflammation of the SMALL vessels (post-capillary venules) of the skin → producing the hallmark PALPABLE PURPURA — histologically a leukocytoclastic vasculitis (purple areas of necrosis / purpura).

The core concept: small-vessel inflammation → red cells + inflammatory debris leak into the dermis → palpable purpura (raised, non-blanching purple spots, classically on the lower legs/dependent areas). Two questions: (1) is this JUST the skin, or SYSTEMIC vasculitis (esp. RENAL — hence “check BP + urine dip”)? and (2) WHAT is the CAUSE? — CSVV is usually secondary (idiopathic ~50%, else infections, drugs, connective tissue disease, cryoglobulinaemia, HSP, malignancy).
The unifying lesion is PALPABLE PURPURA (small-vessel vasculitis) — the key exam sign; distinguish from non-palpable purpura (a bleeding/platelet problem, not vasculitis). Management = treat the cause + supportive, with immunosuppression for severe/systemic disease.

Overview — erythema reactions
Reactive erythematous eruptions — hypersensitivity patterns triggered by infection, drugs or systemic disease. The two classics are erythema multiforme and erythema nodosum.
The organising principle: the morphology + site. EM = target lesions (acral), usually HSV-triggered; EN = tender red nodules on the shins (a panniculitis) with many possible triggers.

What & Why

Erythema multiforme = an acute, usually self-limiting, immune-mediated skin eruption characterised by TARGETOID (“target”) lesions — most often triggered by an INFECTION (classically HSV), not usually a drug.

The core concept — a hypersensitivity reaction: the skin's stereotyped response to a trigger (most commonly herpes simplex virus), producing the pathognomonic target lesion — a concentric three-ring lesion (dusky/blistered centre, pale oedematous middle, erythematous outer ring), classically on the hands + feet (acral, extensor).
Two priorities: (1) recognise the target lesions + acral distribution + identify the trigger (usually HSV, or Mycoplasma in children); (2) — crucially — distinguish it from SJS/TEN (the dangerous, drug-induced, mucosa-severe conditions it superficially resembles). Erythema multiforme is benign + self-limiting — the opposite end of the spectrum from SJS/TEN.

Erythema nodosum = a hypersensitivity PANNICULITIS (inflammation of subcutaneous fat) producing tender, red, raised nodules classically on the SHINS — a REACTIVE cutaneous SIGN of an underlying trigger (drugs, infection, pregnancy, or idiopathic).

The lesions are benign + self-limiting (they resolve over weeks like a deep bruise, without ulceration or scarring) → management is treat the cause + supportive. The clinical work is the investigation for the trigger, not the skin.

DERMATOLOGY__Leg Ulcers & Pressure Injur:
Overview — leg ulcers & pressure injury
Chronic wounds from vascular insufficiency or sustained pressure. Accurate classification drives management.
The organising principle: determine the cause — venous (commonest) vs arterial vs pressure. Always check the ABPI before compression.
TypeFeaturesManagement
Venous ulcergaiter area, shallow, exudative; haemosiderin, lipodermatosclerosisABPI normal → compression
Arterial ulcerdistal/pressure points, punched-out, painful; cold, pulseless leg↓ABPI → vascular referral (do NOT compress)
Pressure sores / ulcersover bony prominences in immobile patients; graded I–IVpressure relief, repositioning, wound care
Check ABPI before applying compression — compression on an arterial ulcer causes ischaemia. Prevent pressure ulcers with repositioning and risk assessment (e.g. Waterlow).
What & Why

Leg ulcers = chronic breaks in the skin below the knee that fail to heal (>2 weeks). The two commonest — VENOUS (~70%) and ARTERIAL — plus NEUROPATHIC (diabetic) and mixed — differ by cause, appearance + location, and the distinction is critical because the management is opposite (venous → compression; arterial → NEVER compress → revascularise).

The core concept — VENOUS vs ARTERIAL is the master decision: compression (the cornerstone of venous ulcer healing) is DANGEROUS (limb-threatening ischaemia) in an arterial ulcer → so every leg ulcer needs an ABPI (ankle-brachial pressure index) before compression, to exclude significant arterial disease.
Venous ulcers arise from chronic venous hypertension (haemosiderin, lipodermatosclerosis, gaiter region); arterial from peripheral arterial disease (distal, punched-out, painful). Pathway: assess → ABPI → classify → treat by type.

ABPI is the KEY test before compression (to exclude arterial disease); + Doppler/duplex (venous incompetence), swab only if infected, screen for diabetes.

  • Avoid routine topical antibiotics/antiseptics — only if clinically infected (NICE NG152)

  • Leg elevation, exercise, weight loss
  • Refer for endovenous ablation (early intervention improves healing + reduces recurrence — the EVRA trial)

🔎 Features
  • Peripheral arterial disease (atherosclerosis) → ischaemia → ulceration; risk = smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, age
  • Deep, punched-out ulcers at distal/pressure sites; PAINFUL (worse on elevation + at night, relieved by hanging the leg down)
  • Cold, pale, shiny, hairless skin, absent pulses; ± claudication/critical limb ischaemia
🚑 Management
  • NEVER compress
  • Urgent VASCULAR referral → revascularisation (angioplasty/stent or bypass); urgent if critical limb ischaemia
  • Cardiovascular risk management: smoking cessation, statin, antiplatelet, blood-pressure + diabetes control, exercise
  • Wound care + analgesia; treat infection

  • Any chronic/atypical non-healing ulcer (rolled/everted edge, abnormal granulation) → biopsy to exclude a Marjolin's ulcer (SCC in a chronic wound)

What & Why

Pressure ulcer (pressure sore, “bedsore”, decubitus ulcer) = localised damage to skin and/or underlying tissue, usually over a BONY PROMINENCE, from sustained PRESSURE (± SHEAR) → ischaemia + tissue death. Largely PREVENTABLE — a key NHS patient-safety/quality marker.

The core concept — PREVENTION dominates: sustained pressure over a bony point → occludes capillaries → ischaemia → necrosis; SHEAR (skin dragged over deep tissue) + moisture/friction accelerate it. Because the mechanism is mechanical + predictable, pressure ulcers are mostly avoidable → priorities: (1) identify at-risk patients + PREVENT, and (2) if one develops, CATEGORISE + treat.
Common in the immobile, elderly, critically ill, neurologically impaired, malnourished; classic sites = sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, greater trochanters (bony prominences).

Mechanism: PRESSURE (capillary occlusion → ischaemia) + SHEAR (deep tissue distortion) + FRICTION + MOISTURE, sustained over a bony prominence → tissue necrosis.

The rule: pressure + shear + moisture + immobility + poor nutrition/perfusion + reduced sensation = pressure ulcer risk. Classic SITES: SACRUM, HEELS, ISCHIAL tuberosities, greater TROCHANTERS, occiput, elbows, malleoli (bony prominences ± device sites).

Risk Assessment & Prevention (NICE CG179)
The principle (NICE CG179): identify at-risk patients EARLY (risk assessment + skin inspection), then PREVENT (reposition, redistribute pressure, skin + nutrition care).
📋 Risk assessment
  • Use a validated tool alongside clinical judgement — Waterlow, Braden, or Norton
  • Assess skin integrity within 6 hours of admission (and on any change)
🛡️ Prevention (the SSKIN bundle)
  • REPOSITION regularly + document the frequency
  • Pressure-redistributing surface (high-spec foam; dynamic for higher risk)
  • Skin inspection + care (clean/dry; barrier products for moisture); optimise nutrition/hydration; heel offloading + device checks
Do NOT: use skin massage/rubbing to prevent ulcers (NICE CG179). The rule: risk-assess (Waterlow + clinical judgement) → REPOSITION + redistributing surface + skin care + nutrition (SSKIN — Surface, Skin inspection, Keep moving, Incontinence/moisture, Nutrition).
Management of an Established Ulcer
The principle: OFFLOAD the pressure + wound care appropriate to the category + optimise the whole patient; involve tissue viability. Continue ALL prevention (the ulcer won't heal under continued pressure).
🩹 Wound care
  • Dressings chosen to manage exudate + promote healing (hydrocolloid/foam/alginate); document surface area (± photography) to track healing
  • DEBRIDEMENT of slough/necrosis (autolytic/sharp) — except stable dry heel eschar
  • No routine systemic antibiotics; treat clinical INFECTION (spreading erythema, cellulitis, systemic upset, suspected osteomyelitis)
👥 Whole patient
  • Optimise nutrition (protein/calories — dietitian)
  • Tissue viability nurse; surgical review (debridement/flap) for large/deep (Cat 3–4) or non-healing
  • Document + report (patient-safety incident); consider safeguarding review (avoidable?)
The rule: offload + continue prevention + wound care (dressings by exudate, debride except heel eschar, treat infection not colonisation) + nutrition + tissue viability/surgery for deep ulcers + document/report.
Complications
Local infection → CELLULITIS, OSTEOMYELITIS (deep ulcers over bone), abscess; SEPSIS; chronic non-healing; pain; rarely Marjolin's ulcer (SCC in a chronic wound); significant morbidity/mortality + cost.
The rule: key complications = infection (cellulitis/osteomyelitis/sepsis), non-healing, pain; deep ulcers over bone → suspect osteomyelitis.

What & Why

Alopecia = hair loss. The two commonest patterns: alopecia areata — an autoimmune, patchy, non-scarring loss — and androgenetic alopecia — the commonest type of alopecia, a hormone- + genetics-driven progressive patterned thinning (“male/female pattern baldness”).

The core concept — SCARRING vs NON-scarring is the master question (it determines reversibility). In non-scarring alopecia (both types + telogen effluvium) the follicle is preserved → potentially reversible/treatable; in scarring (cicatricial) alopecia the follicle is destroyed + replaced by scar → PERMANENT (urgent to recognise).
Within non-scarring: alopecia areata = autoimmune attack on the hair bulb → round bald patches with “exclamation-mark hairs”; androgenetic alopecia = androgen-driven follicle miniaturisation → patterned thinning; telogen effluvium = diffuse shedding after a stressor. Acne vulgaris = a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous unit (the hair follicle + its sebaceous gland) → producing comedones, papules, pustules, cysts/nodules ± scarring — typically on the face, chest and back (the sebaceous-gland-rich areas).

The core concept — four interacting mechanisms at the pilosebaceous follicle: (1) increased sebum (androgen-driven), (2) abnormal follicular keratinisation → the pore blocks → a comedo, (3) colonisation by Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes), and (4) inflammation. This explains the whole lesion spectrum + the treatment logic (each drug targets one or more of these).

Tinea (“ringworm”) = a superficial fungal infection of KERATINISED tissue (skin, hair, nails) caused by DERMATOPHYTES — moulds of Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton. Classified by the body SITE involved (corporis, cruris, pedis, capitis, unguium).

The core concept — dermatophytes live off KERATIN (they digest it) → they infect skin, hair + nails, and both the appearance + name follow the SITE. Two ideas organise the topic: (1) the classic MORPHOLOGY — an annular (“ring”), scaly, erythematous plaque with a raised, advancing SCALY EDGE + CENTRAL CLEARING (the “ring” of ringworm); and (2) the TREATMENT rule that hinges on HAIR or NAIL involvement — topical antifungals CAN'T penetrate the hair follicle or nail plate → so capitis (scalp/hair) + unguium (nails) need ORAL antifungals, whereas skin tinea (corporis/cruris/pedis) responds to TOPICAL.
A crucial trap: topical STEROIDS alter the appearance (tinea incognito) + worsen it → don't treat a scaly rash with steroids without excluding fungus. Reflex: an annular scaly plaque with a raised edge + central clearing = tinea → topical antifungal (or ORAL if hair/nails/extensive). Favoured by warm/humid conditions, shared facilities, animal contact, immunosuppression, diabetes.

Herpes simplex = infection with the herpes simplex virus (HSV-1 or HSV-2) — a DNA herpesvirus causing recurrent grouped vesicles on an erythematous base at mucocutaneous sites. HSV-1 = oral/facial (cold sores) + increasingly genital; HSV-2 = classically genital.

The core concept — LATENCY + REACTIVATION (the herpesvirus hallmark). After a primary infection (often the most severe episode — e.g. gingivostomatitis or a florid first genital episode), the virus travels up the sensory nerve to establish lifelong LATENCY in the sensory (dorsal-root/trigeminal) ganglion → then REACTIVATES periodically (UV, illness, stress, immunosuppression, menstruation) → back down the nerve to produce recurrent lesions at the SAME site, usually milder + preceded by a prodrome (tingling/burning).
Two threads: (1) recognise the grouped vesicles + primary-vs-recurrent pattern, and (2) know the SPECIAL/dangerous presentations — eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow (finger), keratitis (eye), encephalitis (brain), neonatal/immunocompromised HSV. Usually self-limiting, but aciclovir (activated by viral thymidine kinase) treats/suppresses it. Reflex: grouped vesicles on an erythematous base + a tingling prodrome, recurring at the same site = HSV.

Shingles (herpes zoster) = REACTIVATION of latent VARICELLA-ZOSTER VIRUS (VZV) — the same DNA herpesvirus that causes chickenpox (varicella) as the primary infection. After chickenpox, VZV lies dormant in a sensory (dorsal-root/cranial) ganglion, then reactivates to produce clustered vesicles in a DERMATOMAL distribution.

Three threads: (1) recognise the unilateral dermatomal vesicular rash; (2) the biggest complication is POST-HERPETIC NEURALGIA (persistent nerve pain after the rash heals); and (3) the danger sites — OPHTHALMIC zoster (eye — Hutchinson's sign) + RAMSAY HUNT syndrome (ear/facial nerve). A CLINICAL diagnosis (the characteristic umbilicated papules). Consider further workup only in the special contexts: STI screen (adult genital molluscum); HIV test (widespread/atypical/giant molluscum); biopsy only if diagnostic doubt (shows Henderson-Paterson “molluscum bodies”).
Management
The principle: it's benign + SELF-LIMITING → REASSURE + no treatment usually needed; treat only for specific reasons; treat the underlying context.
🛋️ Reassurance (the mainstay)
  • Most cases RESOLVE SPONTANEOUSLY over months (up to ~18 months) without scarring → reassure, avoid aggressive treatment (esp. in children)
  • Advise: avoid scratching/sharing towels (reduce spread/autoinoculation); children need NOT be excluded from school/swimming
✂️ Treat only if indicated
  • Troublesome, extensive, cosmetically/psychologically distressing, or genital in adults
  • Options: cryotherapy, curettage, topical agents (potassium hydroxide, benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, imiquimod) — used selectively; can cause discomfort/scarring
Treat the context: manage co-existing atopic eczema (reduces spread/scratching); HIV/immunosuppression → treat the underlying cause (molluscum often improves with immune restoration/antiretroviral therapy); genital molluscum → sexual health referral + STI screen.

What & Why

Viral warts (verrucae) = common, BENIGN epidermal growths caused by HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUS (HPV) — presenting as keratotic, papillomatous (“warty”) lesions. Different HPV types cause different wart types at different sites (common, plantar, plane, genital).

The core concept — a benign, self-limiting HPV infection of keratinocytes: HPV infects the epidermis → drives keratinocyte proliferation + hyperkeratosis → the rough, warty, papillomatous surface. Most resolve spontaneously (cleared by cell-mediated immunity, often within 1–2 years) — treatment is often optional. Contagious (direct contact + autoinoculation), favouring children, moist/traumatised skin, and the immunocompromised.
Two threads: (1) recognise the type by site + appearance (common/plantar/plane/filiform) and the classic clue — loss of skin lines + thrombosed capillaries (black dots); and (2) know the ONCOGENIC HPV link — genital warts (mostly benign HPV 6/11) vs high-risk oncogenic types (HPV 16/18 → cervical + other cancers). Reflex: a rough, keratotic, papillomatous papule with disrupted skin lines + black dots = viral wart → reassure, often self-resolves.

Impetigo = a common, contagious, SUPERFICIAL bacterial skin infection — usually Staphylococcus aureus (± Streptococcus pyogenes) — classically producing a red, crusted lesion, often on the face of children. The hallmark is a GOLDEN / HONEY-COLOURED CRUST.

The core concept — a superficial epidermal infection (staph/strep colonising + infecting the top layer of skin, often through a small break — a scratch, insect bite, or eczema) → the characteristic honey-coloured crusts. Commonest bacterial skin infection in young children (2–5 years); spread by direct contact/autoinoculation. Reflex: golden/honey-crusted lesions on a child's face = impetigo → hygiene advice + hydrogen peroxide (localised) or antibiotics (widespread/bullous).

DERMATOLOGY__Eczema / Atopic Dermatitis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis) = a chronic, relapsing, inflammatory, itchy red rash — the commonest inflammatory skin disease of childhood, part of the “atopic march” (eczema → asthma → hay fever).

The core concept — a defective skin BARRIER + immune dysregulation: a genetically impaired barrier (classically filaggrin mutations) lets water out (dry skin) + allergens/irritants/microbes in → a Th2-driven inflammatory + itch response → the itch–scratch cycle perpetuates barrier damage. The whole treatment flows from “restore the barrier + damp the inflammation” → EMOLLIENTS (barrier) + TOPICAL STEROIDS (inflammation) are the twin mainstays.
Two threads: (1) the distribution shifts with age (face/extensor in infants → FLEXURES in children/adults); (2) watch for complications — bacterial superinfection + eczema herpeticum. Affects ~10% of children, rarer in adults — most improve with age.

Irritants + allergenssoaps, detergents

The rule: atopic eczema = a genetically defective barrier (filaggrin) + Th2 immune dysregulation, triggered by irritants/allergens/stress; strong atopic family history. Allergens penetrate → inflammation → itch → scratch → more barrier damage (the itch–scratch cycle).
Diagnosis — The UK Criteria

Must have an ITCHY skin condition PLUS ≥3 of the following:

  • Involvement of the FLEXURES (may differ in darker skin types)
  • History of atopy (personal/family — asthma, hay fever, eczema)
  • Persistent DRY skin
  • Onset typically before 2 years old
  • Visible flexural dermatitis (added by the UK Working Party criteria)
The rule: an ITCHY skin condition + ≥3 of (flexural involvement, atopy history, dry skin, onset <2y, visible flexural eczema) = atopic eczema.

DERMATOLOGY__Contact & Seborrhoeic Derma:
Definition & The Core Concept

Contact dermatitis = an eczematous (inflammatory) skin reaction caused by an EXTERNAL substance touching the skin — either an irritant (direct damage) or an allergen (a type IV delayed hypersensitivity). Seborrhoeic dermatitis = a chronic inflammatory dermatitis of the SEBACEOUS (oily) areas, driven by a reaction to the skin commensal yeast Malassezia.

The core concept: both are types of dermatitis/eczema (inflamed, itchy, red, scaly skin), but they differ in WHAT drives them + WHERE they appear — and that is the whole diagnostic key. Contact → an external trigger + a distribution that MATCHES the site of contact (a watch-strap, earrings, gloves, a cream). Seborrhoeic → greasy scaling in the seborrhoeic areas, driven by Malassezia → treated with antifungals (not just steroids).
Both are common, benign and clinically diagnosed; the management overlaps with eczema (emollients, topical steroids) but each has a specific extra step — allergen/irritant avoidance (contact) or antifungals (seborrhoeic).

DERMATOLOGY__Lichen Planus:
Definition & The Core Concept

Lichen planus = a chronic, immune-mediated (T-cell) inflammatory condition affecting the skin, mucous membranes, nails and hair — classically remembered by the P's and its Wickham's striae. Onset age 20–50; usually self-resolving.

The core concept — a T-cell attack on the basal keratinocytes (a “lichenoid” interface reaction) → an intensely itchy, violaceous, flat-topped papular rash. Two ideas capture it: (1) the morphology — the P's (Purple, Pruritic, Polygonal, Planar (flat-topped) Papules/Plaques) with Wickham's striae (fine white surface lines); (2) it's MULTI-SITE → always check other sites (oral, genital, nails, scalp).
Two threads: it can be DRUG-INDUCED (a lichenoid drug eruption) and has a hepatitis C (± B) association. Mostly benign + self-limiting, but erosive oral/genital disease carries a small SCC risk → monitoring. Reflex: itchy, violaceous, flat-topped papules (± white lacy oral lesions) in a 20–50-year-old = lichen planus → check all sites, review drugs, consider hepatitis.

DERMATOLOGY__Psoriasis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Psoriasis = a chronic, immune-mediated, inflammatory skin disease (a family of related diseases) characterised by well-demarcated, salmon-pink plaques with SILVERY scale, driven by accelerated keratinocyte turnover. Chronic plaque psoriasis accounts for >90%.

The core concept — T-cell inflammation → keratinocyte hyperproliferation: the epidermis turns over in days instead of weeks, so cells are shed before maturing → the thick, scaly, well-demarcated plaque. Three ideas organise it: (1) the MORPHOLOGY (salmon-pink plaques + silvery scale on extensor surfaces + scalp, with the Auspitz/Koebner/nail signs); (2) it's SYSTEMIC → psoriatic ARTHRITIS + metabolic/cardiovascular disease + psychological impact; (3) a clear guideline treatment LADDER.
Bimodal onset (late teens + 60–70s); strong genetic component (~30% family history); commoner in Scandinavian populations. Reflex: well-demarcated salmon-pink plaques with silvery scale on elbows/knees/scalp → psoriasis → ask about joints, apply the topical ladder.

Key safety point: systemic steroid WITHDRAWAL can precipitate a pustular/erythrodermic flare → avoid systemic corticosteroids in psoriasis.

The plaque: itchy, well-demarcated, circular-to-oval, bright red/salmon-pink plaques with overlying white/silvery scale, symmetrical, over extensor surfaces + scalp.

DERMATOLOGY__Rosacea:
Definition & The Core Concept

Rosacea = a chronic, relapsing inflammatory skin disease of the FACE — recurrent facial FLUSHING, persistent central ERYTHEMA, TELANGIECTASIA, PAPULES + PUSTULES, and phymatous (rhinophyma) changes. Crucially, it has NO comedones (the key distinction from acne).

The core concept — a chronic inflammatory + vascular disorder of the central face: abnormal vasodilation (flushing → persistent redness → telangiectasia) + inflammation (papules/pustules) ± tissue overgrowth (rhinophyma). Framework: (1) recognise it + separate it from ACNE (rosacea = flushing/erythema/telangiectasia + NO comedones); (2) identify the dominant FEATURE/phenotype — treatment is feature-directed; (3) don't miss OCULAR rosacea (common + sight-threatening).
Common (~10%, underdiagnosed); age 30–50; women more affected but MEN get RHINOPHYMA; Celtic/fair skin, blue eyes most at risk. Reflex: central facial flushing + erythema + papules/pustules WITHOUT comedones in a fair-skinned 30–50-year-old = rosacea.

DERMATOLOGY__Seborrhoeic Keratosis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Seborrhoeic keratosis (basal cell papilloma, “senile wart”) = an extremely common, BENIGN epidermal skin growth — pigmented papules with a waxy, “STUCK-ON” appearance and keratin cysts — harmless, with no need to treat.

The core concept — a benign overgrowth of the epidermis (keratinocytes): the whole clinical importance is recognising it as harmless and distinguishing it from melanoma (its pigmented mimic). Two hallmarks flow from a lesion sitting ON TOP of the skin: a “STUCK-ON”, waxy/warty appearance (as if it could be flicked off), and KERATIN CYSTS (horn cysts/plugs) on the surface + dermoscopy.
Task: confidently identify the benign features → reassure → while staying alert to the rare atypical lesion needing biopsy to exclude melanoma. Very common; increase with age (normal ageing skin); multiple; on the trunk, face + back. Reflex: a well-defined, waxy, “stuck-on” pigmented papule with keratin cysts in an older adult = seborrhoeic keratosis → reassure.

The dermoscopy point: a heavily pigmented seborrhoeic keratosis can mimic melanoma → on dermoscopy it shows reassuring “milia-like cysts” (white keratin cysts) + “comedo-like openings” (± moth-eaten borders) — highly benign features.

  • Colour tan to dark brown/black; often multiple
  • Surface keratin (horn) cysts + a friable, crumbly surface; may itch or catch on clothing
📍 Distribution
  • Trunk, back, face, scalp (not palms/soles)
  • Increase in number with age
The rule: multiple well-defined, waxy, “stuck-on”, warty pigmented papules with keratin cysts on the trunk/face of an older adult = seborrhoeic keratosis.

The sign of Leser-Trélat: the SUDDEN eruption of MULTIPLE seborrhoeic keratoses (a rapid increase in number/size, typically over <1 year) → a PARANEOPLASTIC sign of an internal malignancy (classically GI adenocarcinoma — stomach/colon; also breast, lymphoma) → investigate for underlying cancer.

🛋️ Reassurance
  • Benign + harmless → no treatment needed — the mainstay
✂️ Removal (if indicated)
  • Only if symptomatic (itchy, catching, inflamed), diagnostically uncertain, or for cosmesis
  • Cryotherapy, curettage + cautery, shave excision

DERMATOLOGY__Skin Lesion Morphology & Te:
Definition & The Core Concept

Dermatological terminology = the standardised vocabulary for describing skin lesions — the foundation of every dermatology diagnosis, presentation, and referral. The organising idea: four questions to ask of any rash — MORPHOLOGY, SECONDARY CHANGES, CONFIGURATION, and DISTRIBUTION.

The core concept — dermatology is a visual, pattern-recognition specialty: you can't diagnose (or communicate a referral) without precisely describing what you see. The whole skill is “looking AND seeing” — systematically working through four layers: (1) MORPHOLOGY (the primary lesion — flat or raised? solid or fluid-filled? big or small?); (2) SECONDARY CHANGES (what has happened to the lesion — scale, crust, erosion, lichenification); (3) CONFIGURATION (how lesions are arranged — annular, linear, grouped); and (4) DISTRIBUTION (where on the body — extensor vs flexural, dermatomal, photosensitive).
Getting the vocabulary right turns a rash into a describable pattern → which points to a differential. Reflex: describe every rash as MORPHOLOGY + secondary change + configuration + distribution — e.g. “well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale, in a symmetrical extensor distribution” = psoriasis. This is the descriptive scaffold underpinning every other dermatology note.
The Four-Part Framework

Morphology (primary lesion)What is the fundamental lesion?macule, papule, plaque, vesicle, nodule…

ConfigurationHow are lesions arranged?annular, linear, grouped, serpiginous, target
DistributionWhere on the body?extensor, flexural, dermatomal, photosensitive, acral
The rule: describe every lesion in four steps — MORPHOLOGY → SECONDARY CHANGES → CONFIGURATION → DISTRIBUTION.

The rule: flat colour change = MACULE (<1 cm) or PATCH (>1 cm) — flat, not palpable. Examples: freckle/vitiligo (macule/patch); a café-au-lait patch.

  • sessile (no stalk)

DERMATOLOGY__Cellulitis:
Definition & The Core Concept

Cellulitis = an acute bacterial infection of the DEEP dermis + subcutaneous tissue — usually Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A strep) and/or Staphylococcus aureus — presenting as spreading unilateral erythema, warmth, swelling, and pain. Erysipelas = a more SUPERFICIAL variant (upper dermis + lymphatics) with a sharply demarcated, raised border (usually Strep).

The core concept — a deep, spreading soft-tissue bacterial infection: bacteria enter through a break in the skin barrier (a cut, ulcer, tinea pedis, eczema, insect bite, IV line) → spread through the dermis/subcutis → the four cardinal signs — redness, warmth, swelling, pain — spreading over hours–days, typically UNILATERAL. Framework: (1) recognise it + rule out the DANGEROUS mimic (NECROTISING FASCIITIS); (2) recognise the BENIGN mimics (bilateral “cellulitis” is almost never cellulitis); and (3) grade severity (Eron) to decide oral vs IV + admission, then treat with FLUCLOXACILLIN.
Very common (~1 in 40/year); usually the lower leg. Reflex: spreading unilateral erythema + warmth + swelling + pain = cellulitis → flucloxacillin (oral or IV by severity); check for necrotising fasciitis red flags + treat the entry point.

Risk factors: skin breaks (ulcer/tinea/eczema/wound), LYMPHOEDEMA/venous insufficiency, OBESITY, DIABETES, immunosuppression, previous cellulitis, IV drug use, peripheral vascular disease.
The rule: unilateral hot, red, swollen, tender skin (± fever/lymphangitis), with an entry point (tinea/ulcer/wound), on a risk-factor background (lymphoedema/diabetes/venous disease) = cellulitis.

DERMATOLOGY__Urticaria / Angioedema:
Definition & The Core Concept

Urticaria (“hives”) = transient, itchy WHEALS — hot, acute, itchy weals and plaques due to HISTAMINE release into the skin (transient dermal oedema, pale centre + erythematous rim). Angioedema = the same process but DEEPER — swelling of the dermis/subcutis + mucosa (lips, eyelids, tongue, throat). They often co-exist.

The core concept — a mast-cell–driven condition: mast cells degranulate → release HISTAMINE (± other mediators) → dermal oedema + vasodilation → the itchy wheal. Three axes organise the topic: (1) DEPTH — urticaria (superficial dermis → wheals) vs angioedema (deep dermis/subcutis/mucosa → swelling); (2) DURATION — ACUTE (<6 weeks, often a clear trigger) vs CHRONIC (≥6 weeks, spontaneous/idiopathic or inducible); and (3) the RED-FLAG overlap with ANAPHYLAXIS.
Management is a clean stepwise ANTIHISTAMINE ladder, escalating to omalizumab/immunosuppression for refractory chronic disease. A key “don't miss” is airway angioedema (throat swelling) → anaphylaxis pathway, and a special cause is hereditary/ACE-inhibitor angioedema (bradykinin-mediated, NOT histamine → antihistamines don't work). Reflex: transient itchy wheals = urticaria (histamine) → antihistamine; deeper swelling = angioedema → check the airway + consider anaphylaxis. Each individual wheal is TRANSIENT (<24h) — a key diagnostic feature; the rash migrates.

DERMATOLOGY__Benign Skin Lumps:
What & Why

Dermatofibroma (benign fibrous histiocytoma) = a common, BENIGN skin nodule — a localised proliferation of fibrous/fibrohistiocytic tissue in the dermis — classically arising as scarring following a previous insect bite (or minor skin trauma).

The core concept: essentially a small, benign, firm knot of fibrous tissue in the dermis — a localised over-healing/scar-like reaction to minor trauma. It can be confidently diagnosed clinically by two hallmarks: a firm, pigmented or skin-coloured papule/nodule showing the characteristic “dimple sign” (it dimples inward when pinched). The task is to recognise it as benign (and reassure), while staying alert to features that prompt biopsy to exclude a melanoma.
Common; typically on the legs (esp. young/middle-aged women); usually asymptomatic (occasionally itchy/tender).
The Decisive Fork — Benign Dermatofibroma vs a Concerning Lesion

Dermatofibromas are benign, but the pigmented ones must be distinguished from melanoma:

“dimple sign” positive (dimples on pinching)irregular, changing

The rule: a firm, stable, pigmented-or-skin-coloured nodule (often on the leg, after an insect bite) with a POSITIVE dimple sign = benign dermatofibroma → reassure; change, irregularity, rapid growth, or ulceration → biopsy to exclude melanoma.
The melanoma caveat: a pigmented dermatofibroma can mimic a melanoma → if there is diagnostic doubt (esp. an atypical/changing pigmented lesion), excise/biopsy.
Clinical Features
🔎 Appearance
  • A firm, small (usually 0.5–1 cm) dermal papule/nodule, often on the legs
  • Feels like a hard “pea” or button tethered within the skin
  • Pigmented or skin-coloured; long-standing + stable
🤏 The dimple (Fitzpatrick) sign
  • Squeezing/pinching the lesion laterally causes the centre to DIMPLE inward (it is tethered to the overlying epidermis)
  • The classic diagnostic sign
  • Usually asymptomatic, sometimes itchy or tender
The rule: a firm, tethered, pigmented/skin-coloured nodule on the leg that dimples when pinched = dermatofibroma.

A CLINICAL diagnosis — the firm nodule + positive dimple sign is usually sufficient. Dermoscopy shows a characteristic central white scar-like patch with a peripheral pigment network.
Excision biopsy / histology — only if the diagnosis is uncertain or to exclude melanoma (histology shows a benign dermal fibrohistiocytic proliferation).

🛋️ Reassurance + observation
  • The mainstay — it is benign + harmless, no treatment needed
✂️ Excision
  • Only if symptomatic (persistent itch/pain/catching), diagnostically uncertain (exclude melanoma), or for cosmesis
  • Note: excision leaves a scar and they can recur
The rule: reassure + leave alone (benign); excise only if symptomatic / uncertain / cosmetic.

What & Why

Pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) = a common, BENIGN, rapidly-growing vascular skin lesion — classically a friable nodule that bleeds easily.

The core concept: despite the name it is neither infective (“pyogenic”) nor a true granuloma — it is a benign proliferation of capillaries (a lobular capillary haemangioma), often triggered by minor trauma, pregnancy or hormones. Being a friable ball of blood vessels, it grows rapidly over days–weeks, is bright red, and bleeds profusely with minimal contact.
The single most important point — the ACUTE history: a lesion that appeared + grew quickly fits a pyogenic granuloma, but a chronic, atypical, or pigmented one must be excised to exclude an amelanotic MELANOMA. Have a low threshold to excise + send for histology.
Common on the fingers, hands, lips, gums (esp. in pregnancy — “pregnancy epulis”) and face; often follows minor trauma.

The rule: an ACUTE history (rapid onset) supports a benign pyogenic granuloma; a CHRONIC (or atypical) history → EXCISE to exclude MELANOMA (an amelanotic/nodular melanoma can look identical).
Always send histology: because of the melanoma mimicry, any excised/removed pyogenic granuloma should be sent for histological confirmation.
Clinical Features
🔎 Appearance
  • Rapidly growing (days–weeks), bright/dark red, dome-shaped, shiny nodule
  • Often a collarette of scale at the base
  • Usually small (few mm–1 cm), solitary, painless
🩸 Behaviour + triggers
  • Friable → bleeds profusely with minor trauma/contact (recurrent bleeding — the classic complaint)
  • Sites: fingers/hands, lips, gums, face
  • Triggers: minor trauma, PREGNANCY (gum lesion = “pregnancy epulis”), hormones, certain drugs (e.g. retinoids)
The rule: a rapidly-growing, bright-red, friable nodule that bleeds easily (often on a finger/lip, after minor trauma or in pregnancy) = pyogenic granuloma.

A CLINICAL diagnosis (the acute history + the friable bleeding nodule).
Histology after removal: excise + send for histology — to confirm the diagnosis + exclude an amelanotic melanoma (esp. if chronic/atypical).

Management
The principle: remove it (excise/curette + cautery) + send for histology; excise any chronic/atypical lesion to exclude melanoma.
✂️ Removal
  • Curettage + cautery (base cauterised to reduce bleeding/recurrence), shave excision, or full excision — specimen sent for histology
  • Other options: silver nitrate, cryotherapy, laser
Key points
  • Chronic/atypical → excise to exclude melanoma (histology)
  • Pregnancy-related lesions often regress after delivery → may be managed conservatively
  • Can recur after treatment (esp. incomplete removal)
The rule: excise/curette + cautery + histology; excise chronic/atypical lesions to exclude melanoma; pregnancy lesions may regress post-partum.

What & Why

Keloid scar = an abnormal, excessive scar in which fibrous tissue overgrows BEYOND the boundaries of the original wound — arising spontaneously or following trauma — on characteristic sites (chest, upper back, neck, abdomen).

The core concept: normal healing lays down collagen then stops; in a keloid that “stop” signal fails → fibroblasts keep producing collagen → the scar grows OUTWARD, beyond the wound margins (the defining difference from a hypertrophic scar, which stays within the wound). As a disorder of over-healing it can appear after any injury (even piercings, acne, surgery, vaccination), favours high-tension/sternal sites, is commoner + more severe in darker skin + younger patients, and tends to RECUR after excision (cutting one out is another wound → another keloid).
Usually a cosmetic concern, but may be asymptomatic, painful, or itchy.
The Decisive Fork — Keloid vs Hypertrophic Scar

Both are excessive scars, but they differ in one defining way — do they extend beyond the wound?

Regressiondoes NOT regress (persists/grows)often regresses/flattens over time

The rule: keloid = scar EXTENDS BEYOND the original wound + doesn't regress + recurs after excision; hypertrophic scar = stays WITHIN the wound + tends to regress.
The recurrence point: a keloid recurs (often worse) if simply excised → excision is usually combined with an adjuvant (intralesional steroid, radiotherapy) to reduce recurrence.
Risk Factors
🧬 Who
  • Darker skin types (Fitzpatrick IV–VI) — much commoner + more severe
  • Younger patients (10–30s); family history / genetic predisposition
📍 Where
  • High-tension / sternal sites — chest, shoulders, upper back, neck, earlobes, jawline
  • Any skin injury: surgery, piercings, acne, burns, vaccination, lacerations
The rule: keloids favour darker skin, younger patients, a family history, and high-tension sites (chest/upper back/neck/shoulders/earlobes).

What & Why

Xanthelasma (xanthelasma palpebrarum) = soft, yellowish plaques of lipid deposition on the eyelids — the commonest type of xanthoma (cutaneous lipid deposits) — and clinically important as a possible sign of raised cholesterol.

The core concept: collections of lipid-laden macrophages (foam cells) in the eyelid dermis — so their significance is as a potential external marker of a lipid abnormality. The key balance: they are indicative of raised cholesterol BUT are often idiopathic (up to ~50% have NORMAL lipids). Task: (1) don't assume — CHECK a lipid profile + cardiovascular risk; (2) reassure that the lesions themselves are benign + harmless.
Common in middle-aged/older adults; located at the medial (inner) canthus of the upper (± lower) eyelids, often symmetrical. Independently associated with a modestly increased cardiovascular risk even when lipids are normal.
The Decisive Fork — Is There an Underlying Lipid Abnormality?

The whole point of spotting a xanthelasma is to check the lipids — because it may (or may not) signal dyslipidaemia:

Secondary to dyslipidaemiaIdiopathic (normolipaemic)
Lipidsraised (↑cholesterol/LDL)NORMAL (“often idiopathic”)
Causefamilial hypercholesterolaemia, secondary hyperlipidaemianone identified
Frequency~half~half
Actiontreat the lipids + CV riskreassure (± treat cosmetically)
The rule: xanthelasma → CHECK a fasting lipid profile → if raised, manage the dyslipidaemia + cardiovascular risk; if normal, reassure.
The familial hypercholesterolaemia point: xanthelasma (esp. if young / with tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus, a strong family history of early cardiovascular disease) should prompt consideration of familial hypercholesterolaemia.
Clinical Features
🟡 The lesion
  • Soft, well-demarcated, yellow / yellow-orange plaques or papules
  • At the medial canthus of the upper eyelids, often bilateral + symmetrical
  • Flat or slightly raised, painless; slowly enlarge/persist; middle-aged+ adults
👀 Look for hyperlipidaemia signs
  • Corneal arcus (esp. if <45 yrs → significant)
  • Tendon xanthomas (Achilles, knuckles) → familial hypercholesterolaemia
  • Eruptive/tuberous xanthomata → hypertriglyceridaemia / mixed hyperlipidaemia
The rule: soft symmetrical yellow eyelid plaques at the medial canthus = xanthelasma → examine for corneal arcus + tendon xanthomas → check lipids.

Investigations
Fasting lipid profile — total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides — the key test (may reveal treatable dyslipidaemia).
Cardiovascular risk assessment (e.g. QRISK) + screen for secondary causes of hyperlipidaemia (hypothyroidism — TFTs, diabetes, liver/renal disease); consider familial hypercholesterolaemia (family history, young age, tendon xanthomas).
Management
The principle: treat the underlying dyslipidaemia + cardiovascular risk if present; the lesions themselves are benign → remove only for cosmesis (and they recur).
🩺 Treat the underlying cause (priority)
  • If lipids are raised → manage the dyslipidaemia: lifestyle (diet, weight, exercise) + statins as indicated
  • Treat any secondary cause / familial hypercholesterolaemia + optimise cardiovascular risk
💅 Cosmetic removal
  • Benign — remove only for cosmesis: surgical excision, laser, cryotherapy, chemical cautery (e.g. trichloroacetic acid)
  • They commonly RECUR (esp. if the dyslipidaemia is untreated)
The rule: treat the lipids/CV risk if abnormal; remove the plaques only for cosmesis (they recur); reassure they're benign.
